scoreNote: Strong (5): engages both halves of the statement, grants the power of praise, and then shows persuasively why ignoring negative actions fails students; concrete classroom examples and a balanced, well-controlled argument.

sentences.text: Anyone who has watched a hesitant child light up at a few words of encouragement understands the extraordinary power of praise.

Some educators distil that observation into a rule for all teaching: that the surest method is to praise positive actions and to ignore negative ones entirely, on the theory that attention rewards whatever it touches.

Praise should indeed sit at the heart of good teaching, but the instruction to ignore negative actions altogether goes too far, since students who are never corrected are denied the very feedback that improvement requires.

sections.role: Body — Where the statement holds true

sentences.text: It is true that the first half of the claim rests on solid ground.
A child repeatedly scolded for clumsy handwriting often concludes, not unreasonably, that writing is simply something she cannot do, and gives up before she has fairly begun.

Praising what she manages well, by contrast, supplies the confidence and motivation on which any further effort depends, and decades of research suggest that encouragement outperforms the fear of punishment over the long run.
Even adults respond this way, working harder for a manager who notices their successes than for one who points only at their failures.
To this extent, a teacher who leads with praise rather than criticism is usually closer to the truth than one who does the reverse.
However, to ignore negative actions completely is to mistake kindness for neglect.
A student who keeps solving the same equation the same wrong way will go on doing so indefinitely unless someone interrupts the pattern and shows a better path.
Silence in the face of error is not generosity; it abandons the learner to rehearse a mistake until it sets, like cement, into a permanent habit.

Worse still, to overlook genuinely harmful behavior — cheating, dishonesty, cruelty toward classmates — teaches the entire room that such conduct carries no consequences, a lesson far more damaging than any spelling error.
Students are remarkably quick to read what a teacher chooses to ignore, and they adjust their own behavior to match that silent signal.
A teacher who never corrects has not spared her students; she has quietly failed them.
The resolution lies in recognizing that the real question is not whether to address negative actions but how.
Correction offered gently, as an invitation to solve a problem rather than a verdict on the student's worth, repairs the error without wounding the person.
Understood this way, criticism becomes an extension of encouragement rather than its enemy, and the two work as partners instead of rivals.
Tone, timing, and trust are what separate the correction that motivates from the criticism that merely stings, and a skilled teacher attends to all three.
The aim is never to humiliate but to inform, so that the student leaves the exchange knowing exactly how to do better next time.
What students need is not the absence of correction but its presence in a constructive, humane form.
In conclusion, the statement is half right and half dangerous.
Praise should be the foundation on which a classroom is built, but ignoring negative actions would strip students of the guidance that turns effort into genuine progress.
The finest teachers do not choose between encouragement and correction; they offer both, praising generously and correcting with care.
